title: Noor and the Undertow
premise: Sable Joubert, a restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after his mother's death, drifts through her funeral numb to grief and flavor alike. A stranger named Yolande greets the mourners with the word 'Noor'—a name from his mother's first life in Mauritius that no one in the family has ever spoken. As the deadline looms to sell the family house, Sable follows Yolande's trail back to Port Louis, uncovering that his mother had another family, another name, and a debt of loyalty she spent thirty years repaying in secret. In the end Sable chooses truth over inheritance: he tells both families everything, keeps only his mother's recipe notebook instead of the house, and tastes salt for the first time in years standing in the Indian Ocean.
about_author: Ada Almeida is the pen name of a former food writer who grew up between Lisbon and Port Louis and writes about families that keep their histories in kitchens. 'Noor and the Undertow' is her second novel.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Weeks before his mother's funeral, Sable files restaurant reviews he cannot taste, eats dinner alone like a man renting his own life, and signs papers to sell the family house without reading them. The emotional beat is hollow competence: he functions perfectly and feels nothing, establishing the numbness the novel must break.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Sable's POV at the funeral. Amid casseroles he can't taste, a stranger named Yolande embraces him and calls his mother 'Noor Joubert'—a name his aunt visibly flinches at. When Sable asks, everyone changes the subject. The beat is the first crack: curiosity piercing grief, and the discovery that invisibility was a choice made for him.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Alternating Sable's POV with fragments of his mother's letters found in the attic. Clearing the house for sale, Sable finds a locked tin, a photograph of his mother with an unknown child, and letters addressed to 'Noor.' His sister Priya urges him to burn it all and close escrow. The beat is loyalty pulling against truth within the family itself.

chapters.title: Yolande
chapters.summary: Yolande's POV. The stranger reveals herself as his mother's childhood friend, now dying, who promised Noor she'd come say goodbye properly. She gives Sable half a story: a betrayal in Port Louis, a debt, a name abandoned on purpose. She refuses to finish it unless he comes to Mauritius himself. The beat is being handed a key he didn't ask for.

chapters.title: Escrow
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. The buyer's agent pressures him to sign; Priya needs the money; Sable stalls, lying badly about why. He cooks his mother's recipes from memory and tastes nothing, which frightens him more than the secrets do. The beat is rising pressure—the sale becomes a clock ticking against the truth.

chapters.title: The Long Way to Port Louis
chapters.summary: Sable's POV en route and arriving. He defies Priya, flies to Mauritius, and finds a street where older residents still call a shuttered creole restaurant 'Noor's place.' Yolande meets him at the airport and takes him past the house where his mother grew up. The beat is disorientation turning into hunger—he wants the whole story now.

chapters.title: The Other Family
chapters.summary: Yolande's POV delivering the revelation. Noor had a sister, Anjali, whose son Sable's mother raised money for—and then, after a fire that killed Anjali's husband, took the blame for, letting herself be cast out under the name Noor so the family could survive intact elsewhere. Sable has cousins alive today. The beat is vertigo: his identity was built on someone else's sacrifice.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. He meets his cousin Dev, who wants nothing from him except that the lie stay buried—Anjali's children built lives on their father's honorable memory. Meanwhile Priya calls: the buyer will walk unless Sable signs tomorrow. Torn between two families' peace and one truth, Sable walks into the ocean at night. The beat is the darkest hour, grief finally breaking open.

chapters.title: Salt
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, climax. In the water he tastes salt—his first taste in two years—and understands his tongue closed when his mother's truth did. He returns, signs nothing, and instead gathers both families: he reads his mother's letters aloud to Priya by phone and to Dev in person, refusing to let anyone inherit the silence. The beat is costly honesty, chosen over belonging-by-omission.

chapters.title: Noor's Table
chapters.summary: Sable's POV, resolution. The house sells anyway, but Sable keeps the tin of recipes and co-opens a small Sunday supper club with Dev called Noor's Table, cooking his mother's dishes with Anjali's corrections written in the margins. He writes his last review honestly, then resigns. The final beat: belonging rebuilt on truth, and a man who owns his life again.
